chunks: Al-Fudayl ibn Yasar narrated, he said: I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)
I said: I entered with Umrah, so where should I cut the Talbiyah? He said: At the pass of the Medinians. I said: Where is the pass of the Medinians? He said: At the place of the Cloth-dyers.

This narration is specifically for one who came to Mecca via the route of Medina. And the narration in which he said that he cuts it at Dhi Tuwa is for one who came via the route of Iraq. And the narration that included cutting it when facing the Kaaba is for one who had left Mecca for Umrah.
And there is no contradiction between these reports, according to what some people thought, and attributed that to choice (takhayyur).

key_terms.التَّخْيِيرِ: Choice or option, implying flexibility rather than contradiction
key_terms.التَّلْبِيَةَ: The ritual proclamation of 'Labbayk' recited during Hajj and Umrah
key_terms.ذِي طُوًى: Dhi Tuwa, a location near Mecca mentioned in Quran and Hadith
key_terms.عَقَبَةِ الْمَدَنِيِّينَ: The Pass of the Medinians, a specific location near Mecca

ai.seo_question: Where should a pilgrim stop reciting the Talbiyah when entering Mecca for Umrah?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi resolves apparent contradictions in the hadith literature by contextualizing the specific stopping points for ending the Talbiyah according to the pilgrim's entry route—whether from Medina, Iraq, or within Mecca itself. This demonstrates the Shia scholarly principle of reconciling narrations through geographical specificity rather than viewing them as conflicting or merely permissive alternatives.
